observations.prompt:
An input element #x exists in the following markup:

<fieldset disabled id="fs">
  <legend>Title</legend>
  <input id="x" type="text" disabled required value="">
</fieldset>

A script then runs:
  document.getElementById('x').removeAttribute('disabled');

After the script executes, what is the effective state of #x?

observations.prompt: A disabled outer fieldset's first legend contains a disabled inner fieldset that has no legend child. Inside the inner fieldset is <input id='x'> with no own disabled attribute. Which statement correctly describes #x's disabled status and why?

Consider this HTML structure:

<fieldset disabled>
  <legend>
    <fieldset disabled>
      <legend><input id="A"></legend>
      <input id="B">
    </fieldset>
  </legend>
  <input id="C">
</fieldset>

None of the inputs have their own disabled attribute. Which correctly describes the effective disabled state of A, B, and C?
<input id='c' type='email' value='bad' required> is inside a disabled fieldset and not inside any legend. What do c.willValidate and c.checkValidity() return?
<input id='b' disabled> sits inside a disabled fieldset, not inside any legend element. A script executes b.removeAttribute('disabled'). What is the effective state of #b afterward?

Given this markup:

<fieldset disabled>
  <input id="q" type="email" value="not-an-email" required>
</fieldset>

The input #q has an invalid email value and is required. A script reads q.willValidate and then calls q.checkValidity(). What are the results?
